introduction: This report describes patterns in how you answered 120 personality statements. Treat each interpretation as a starting point to check against your experience. Your five broad traits bring together more specific facets, so a single trait score can hide meaningful differences. Work and everyday-life suggestions are optional experiments: keep what helps, adjust what does not, and consider the situation as well as your preferences.
limitations: Scores summarize your own answers at this time. Mood, recent experiences, language, and the setting can affect responses; this report is not a fixed definition of you.

Lower, middle, and higher describe your keyed response mean on the 1–5 scale. The editorial bands are below 2.5, 2.5 through 3.5 inclusive, and above 3.5. They are not population rankings, percentiles, or validated cutoffs.
This is an adult self-reflection report, not a clinical assessment. Facets called Anxiety and Depression do not establish a mental health condition or rule one out.
No trait level is universally better. Strengths and difficulties depend on your responsibilities, relationships, resources, and environment.
Work suggestions do not predict performance, select a career, or establish suitability for employment. Life suggestions are editorial hypotheses, not validated interventions or treatment advice.
Each facet uses four items. Read small score differences cautiously, especially near a band boundary; no confidence interval or reliable-change estimate is provided.

Intellect does not measure IQ, Morality does not measure moral worth, and Liberalism does not identify a political party. These are historical facet labels with narrower meanings explained in the report.
The report uses predefined editorial rules. It does not infer a unique personality type, diagnose you, or make validated predictions from combinations of traits.

Some Liberalism items directly concern political beliefs and originate in a particular cultural context. Treat these answers as sensitive. A Norwegian translation does not establish cultural equivalence or Norwegian norms.

Comparisons between facets describe raw response means, not how unusual a tendency is. Facets differ in content and endorsement rates; without suitable norms, the highest mean cannot establish your strongest trait relative to other people.

N.name: Emotional reactivity (Neuroticism)
N.description: This trait summarizes reported tendencies toward worry, emotional discomfort, and feeling overwhelmed. Its facets cover different experiences; a broad score should not replace reading those details. A higher response mean is not a diagnosis, and a lower mean does not mean you never experience distress.

low.meaning: Your answers lean away from statements about frequent worry and emotional disruption. You may often feel steady when plans change, although particular situations can still affect you strongly. Check which facets fit rather than assuming calmness in every setting.
low.strength: A steady response can make it easier to stay with a practical problem during uncertainty. Others may value your ability to pause and identify the next manageable action.
low.watch: Your own level of concern may differ from someone else's. Moving quickly to solutions can leave their feelings unacknowledged, even when your intention is to help.
low.work: When a colleague raises a risk, ask what evidence they see before deciding it is minor. Pair your calm response with an explicit check of deadlines, consequences, and responsibilities.
low.life: In a difficult conversation, try naming what the other person seems concerned about before offering reassurance. A calm tone works best when it also communicates attention.
low.experiment: For one week, choose one tense moment each day and record what you noticed, what you checked, and whether your first assessment changed. Use the examples to refine your judgment.

middle.meaning: Your answers sit around the middle of the response scale for emotional reactivity. You may recognize some worry or sensitivity alongside periods of steadiness. Different situations or sharply different facet scores could produce this same average.
middle.strength: You may find occasions when concern prompts preparation and others when you can let uncertainty remain unresolved. Look for specific examples of each rather than assuming a consistent balance.
middle.watch: An average can hide recurring pressure points. A demanding deadline, social evaluation, or lack of sleep may matter more to your experience than the broad label suggests.
middle.work: Identify the two work situations that tend to create the most friction. Decide in advance what information, preparation, or support would make each easier to handle.
middle.life: Let close people know what helps when you are under pressure. Preferences can vary: sometimes you may want practical help, and sometimes space to describe the problem.
middle.experiment: Track three stressful and three manageable situations this week. Note the demands, available support, and your response. Look for a repeatable difference before changing your routine.

high.meaning: Your answers lean toward experiencing worry, emotional discomfort, or pressure. Some events may stay with you longer than you would like. Review the facets to see which experiences drive this pattern; the score does not establish a disorder.
high.strength: Your concern may sometimes draw attention to an unresolved issue or a need for preparation. Whether it helps depends on the situation and the accuracy of the concern, not the score alone.
high.watch: A strong feeling can make an uncertain outcome seem more certain. It may help to separate what happened, what you fear could happen, and what information is still missing.
high.work: For ambiguous requests, clarify the desired result and the next checkpoint. A short written agreement may reduce repeated guessing about whether you are meeting expectations.
high.life: When a conversation feels loaded, consider asking for a brief pause and a clear time to return. Explain what you need without assuming you know the other person's intention.
high.experiment: Choose one manageable recurring concern. Write down the observable facts, one unanswered question, and one small action within your control. Later, compare the anticipated outcome with what actually happened.

E.name: Extraversion
E.description: Extraversion covers social engagement, assertiveness, activity, excitement seeking, and positive emotional expression. Enjoying company, speaking up, and enjoying stimulation are related but distinct preferences. A lower mean does not establish shyness or poor social skills.

low.meaning: Your answers lean toward a quieter or less outwardly active style. You may prefer smaller groups, fewer competing demands, or more time to form a response. Your facet scores can show whether this is mainly about company, pace, or stimulation.
low.strength: A preference for less stimulation can support deliberate attention and conversations with room for detail. These are possibilities to check in your own experience, not abilities established by a score.
low.watch: When a group rewards immediate contributions, useful thoughts can remain unheard. Other people may also mistake a quiet style for disinterest if they have little information about your preferences.
low.work: Ask for the agenda before a discussion and prepare one point you want to contribute. Written follow-up can give your ideas another route into the decision.
low.life: Explain the kinds of social time you enjoy. Suggest a walk, a small dinner, or a defined visit rather than leaving others to interpret a declined invitation.
low.experiment: Try one small-group activity and one quieter activity this week. Note your enjoyment and energy afterward. Use that evidence to plan your next social commitment.

middle.meaning: Your response mean falls in the middle band for extraversion. You may enjoy social contact in some settings and prefer quiet in others. The average can also reflect strong preferences in opposite directions across the facets.
middle.strength: You may have examples of enjoying both collaboration and independent time. Identifying the conditions that support each is more useful than expecting yourself to switch comfortably in every situation.
middle.watch: A schedule can accumulate more interaction or solitude than you intended. Your preferred mix may shift with the activity, the people involved, and other demands on your attention.
middle.work: Group related meetings where possible, then leave room to complete the work they create. Notice whether your best contributions come during discussion, preparation, or later reflection.
middle.life: Before accepting another invitation, consider what the rest of the week already contains. Make room for both connection and the amount of unstructured time you find useful.
middle.experiment: For five days, note the amount and kind of interaction you had and how you felt afterward. Change one element next week and check whether the adjustment helps.

high.meaning: Your answers lean toward active engagement with people, expression, or stimulation. You may enjoy exchanging ideas aloud and having things happening around you. Check the facets: social warmth, assertiveness, and excitement seeking need not be equally prominent.
high.strength: Your willingness to engage may help start conversations and make participation easier for others. It can be useful when a task benefits from visible energy, outreach, or quick exchange.
high.watch: Enthusiasm can occupy more conversational space than you intended. A lively interaction may feel productive even when the group has not clarified a decision or heard quieter perspectives.
high.work: Use your participation to invite specific contributions from others. After a discussion, state the decision, the owner, and the next step so momentum turns into follow-through.
high.life: Check whether someone wants an energetic exchange, quiet company, or time alone. Differences in social appetite need not imply differences in affection or commitment.
high.experiment: In three conversations, ask a question and leave a full pause before adding your own view. Note whether you hear anything you would otherwise have missed.

O.name: Openness
O.description: Openness covers imagination, aesthetic interests, attention to feelings, willingness to try unfamiliar activities, intellectual exploration, and questioning convention. It describes reported preferences, not intelligence, expertise, creativity as an achievement, or political identity.

low.meaning: Your answers lean toward familiar, concrete, or established approaches. You may prefer an idea with a clear practical purpose over exploration for its own sake. Individual facets can reveal areas where you are much more curious or adventurous.
low.strength: A preference for what is clear and proven can help keep attention on practical needs. You may find satisfaction in refining a familiar approach and making it dependable for the people using it.
low.watch: An unfamiliar option can look less useful simply because its benefits are harder to picture. Check the evidence before treating novelty itself as a reason to dismiss an idea.
low.work: When a new approach is proposed, ask which problem it solves and what a small trial would show. This can make a change easier to evaluate on concrete terms.
low.life: Keep the routines you value while making a little room for another person's interests. A shared new experience can be small and bounded rather than a major disruption.
low.experiment: Choose one low-cost variation on a familiar activity. Decide beforehand what would make it worthwhile, try it once, and compare the experience with your expectation.

middle.meaning: Your response mean lies in the middle band for openness. You may seek novelty in selected areas while preferring familiar approaches elsewhere. Read the facets to distinguish intellectual curiosity, imagination, aesthetics, and willingness to change routines.
middle.strength: You may have examples of combining an established method with one new element. That can be useful when a situation calls for exploration without replacing everything that already works.
middle.watch: Your appetite for novelty may depend on the subject. Do not assume that enjoying new ideas means enjoying changes to your schedule, or that familiar routines imply little curiosity.
middle.work: For a decision with several options, compare one established approach with one alternative. Use the same criteria for both, including effort, uncertainty, and the problem you need to solve.
middle.life: Tell others where you enjoy surprise and where advance notice helps. Specific preferences are easier to accommodate than a broad claim that you are either spontaneous or routine-oriented.
middle.experiment: Pick one routine to keep and one to vary this week. Record what each choice contributed. Use that comparison to make the next choice deliberately.

high.meaning: Your answers lean toward imagination, exploration, or interest in unfamiliar perspectives. You may enjoy considering possibilities beyond the immediate task. The facets show which forms of openness matter most to you; this score does not establish superior insight.
high.strength: An appetite for exploration may help you notice alternatives and ask questions that reopen a stuck discussion. Your ideas become especially useful when you connect them to the situation's practical needs.
high.watch: A new possibility can compete with finishing an existing commitment. Others may also need more explanation or evidence before an idea that feels exciting to you feels workable to them.
high.work: Separate time for generating options from time for choosing and completing one. State the problem, the proposed change, and the smallest useful way to test it.
high.life: Invite others into your interests without assuming they want the same amount of novelty. Agree on which shared routines provide stability and which are open to experimentation.
high.experiment: Select one idea from your current list and give it a small, finishable form. Record what completing it taught you that further thinking alone had not resolved.

A.name: Agreeableness
A.description: Agreeableness covers trust, straightforwardness, helping, cooperation, modesty, and sympathetic concern. It describes tendencies in relating to others, not goodness, moral worth, relationship quality, or the absence of healthy disagreement.

low.meaning: Your answers lean toward a more skeptical, competitive, or self-assertive interpersonal style. You may be willing to question motives or challenge a proposal. Check the facets before assuming these tendencies apply equally to trust, compassion, and cooperation.
low.strength: A readiness to question can be useful when a group needs scrutiny or a clear statement of competing interests. It helps most when your challenge is specific and grounded in the issue.
low.watch: A direct challenge may be heard as a judgment of the person. If others become defensive, it can become harder to obtain the information needed to resolve the disagreement.
low.work: State the shared objective before identifying a concern. Ask what evidence would change each person's view, including your own, so the discussion has a route toward resolution.
low.life: When you disagree, describe the behavior and its effect rather than assigning a motive. Make room for the possibility that the other person understood the situation differently.
low.experiment: In one disagreement, summarize the other person's position until they confirm you understood it. Then make your request. Note whether the conversation becomes clearer, even if agreement does not follow.

middle.meaning: Your answers fall in the middle band for agreeableness. You may value cooperation while also being willing to protect your interests. This mean can represent different mixtures of trust, helping, modesty, and willingness to compromise.
middle.strength: You may have examples of both accommodating another person and holding your ground. Examining what guided those choices can help you make future decisions more intentional and easier to explain.
middle.watch: Your response may change with the stakes or the relationship. Others can find it difficult to predict your boundaries if those boundaries become visible only after you are frustrated.
middle.work: Before a negotiation, identify what is essential, what is flexible, and what you need to understand. This makes it easier to cooperate without losing track of your responsibilities.
middle.life: Make requests and limits specific. Saying what you can offer, when you can offer it, and what you cannot take on gives others usable information.
middle.experiment: Review one recent yes and one recent no. For each, identify the need you were protecting and whether you communicated it clearly. Try clearer wording in your next similar conversation.

high.meaning: Your answers lean toward trust, cooperation, or concern for others. You may place substantial weight on maintaining goodwill and responding to people's needs. The facets help distinguish compassion from other tendencies, such as modesty or avoiding confrontation.
high.strength: Your willingness to help and consider another perspective may support constructive relationships. It is most sustainable when expectations are clear and you also have room to express your own needs.
high.watch: Agreeing quickly can hide a practical limit or an important disagreement. A request that seems small in the moment may become difficult when added to commitments others cannot see.
high.work: Before accepting additional work, check capacity and priorities. Offer a realistic scope or timing, and surface a concern early enough for the team to act on it.
high.life: Treat a clear limit as useful information in a relationship. You can acknowledge another person's disappointment while still explaining what you are able to do.
high.experiment: Use one warm, specific boundary this week: acknowledge the request, state your limit, and offer an alternative only if you want to. Reflect on the actual response rather than the response you feared.

C.name: Conscientiousness
C.description: Conscientiousness covers perceived effectiveness, order, responsibility, striving, persistence, and deliberation. It describes reported habits and preferences. It does not establish competence, personal value, or how reliably someone will perform in every environment.

low.meaning: Your answers lean away from highly structured planning or sustained task control. You may prefer flexibility, act spontaneously, or find some obligations difficult to organize. The facets distinguish orderliness, persistence, striving, and other parts of this pattern.
low.strength: A lighter attachment to plans may leave room to adapt when circumstances change. Check whether this flexibility helps in your actual situation and where a little structure would protect important commitments.
low.watch: Tasks with delayed rewards or several small steps may be easy to postpone. Relying on memory can also make an intention less visible at the moment you need to act.
low.work: Give one important task a visible next action and a realistic time to begin. Agree on checkpoints for longer work so a delay can be noticed while adjustment is still possible.
low.life: Use a simple reminder for one recurring obligation. Choose a system you will actually see and maintain rather than building a complicated routine that creates more work.
low.experiment: For five days, choose one small priority each morning and define what finished means. Record whether you completed it and what made starting easier or harder.

middle.meaning: Your response mean is in the middle band for conscientiousness. You may use structure in some areas and a looser approach in others. A tidy environment, strong ambition, and steady follow-through are distinct facets and need not move together.
middle.strength: You may have experience using plans when they help and adjusting them when circumstances change. Identify where that approach has worked rather than assuming the average describes every responsibility.
middle.watch: A system that works for an interesting project may be less effective for routine maintenance. Notice whether particular kinds of tasks repeatedly fall outside your usual planning habits.
middle.work: Match the amount of structure to the consequence of a missed step. A simple checklist may be enough for a repeatable task, while a complex handoff needs explicit ownership and timing.
middle.life: Choose a few recurring commitments that deserve reliable reminders. Leave flexibility elsewhere so planning supports what matters without filling every available hour.
middle.experiment: Compare one task you finished smoothly with one you postponed. Note clarity, timing, interest, and interruptions. Apply one helpful condition from the first task to the next difficult one.

high.meaning: Your answers lean toward planning, responsibility, or sustained effort. You may like clear expectations and take commitments seriously. Read the facets to see whether this pattern is driven more by order, achievement striving, persistence, or careful deliberation.
high.strength: Your attention to preparation and follow-through may help turn intentions into completed work. It is particularly useful when responsibilities are clear and the level of detail matches the consequences of an error.
high.watch: Additional checking or effort can continue after it stops adding much value. Changes to a plan may also feel disruptive when you have invested heavily in making it work.
high.work: Agree on completion criteria before starting. Distinguish essential quality checks from optional polish, and revisit priorities when new work arrives rather than absorbing every request into the original plan.
high.life: Leave some shared time open to other people's preferences. Explain which commitments matter most to you while allowing less consequential routines to vary.
high.experiment: For one low-stakes task, set a time limit and a clear standard for completion. Stop when that standard is met, then check whether extra effort would actually have changed the outcome.

N1.name: Anxiety
N1.description: Reported tendency to anticipate threats or feel worried; this facet is not a clinical anxiety assessment.
N1.low: You endorsed fewer worry-related statements. Check important risks explicitly even when you feel comfortable.
N1.high: You endorsed more worry-related statements. Try separating a concrete concern from an unanswered question before deciding what to do.
N1.middle: Worry may depend on how uncertain or consequential a situation feels. Compare a familiar task with an unfamiliar one.
N1.work: For an uncertain task, write down the specific risk and the next piece of information you need.
N1.life: Compare how you react to a familiar plan and an unexpected change.

N2.name: Anger
N2.description: Reported tendency to feel irritated or angry when things go wrong; it does not establish aggressive behavior.
N2.low: You report relatively little irritation. If a problem matters, state it clearly even when you do not feel angry.
N2.high: You report more irritation. Notice the specific unmet expectation and consider expressing a request once you can do so clearly.
N2.middle: Irritation may arise around particular frustrations rather than across your whole day. Notice which expectations matter most.
N2.work: When a process frustrates you, describe the obstacle and request one change.
N2.life: In a disagreement, name the expectation that was not met before deciding how to respond.

N3.name: Depression
N3.description: A historical facet label for reported discouragement, sadness, or low spirits; it cannot diagnose or rule out depression.
N3.low: You endorsed fewer low-spirited statements. This does not mean every period of life feels easy or positive.
N3.high: You endorsed more low-spirited statements. Consider your recent circumstances when interpreting this result; it is not a clinical conclusion.
N3.middle: Your answers do not point consistently toward either end of the low-spirits scale. Recent circumstances may help explain the variation.
N3.work: Consider how your current circumstances affect motivation; this score does not establish a health condition.
N3.life: Notice whether the answers fit your usual experience or a particularly difficult recent period.

N4.name: Self-Consciousness
N4.description: Reported discomfort with social evaluation or being the focus of attention.
N4.low: You report less discomfort with being noticed. Others may need more preparation before being put on the spot.
N4.high: You report more discomfort with evaluation. Preparing one contribution in advance may make a specific social task feel more manageable.
N4.middle: Being noticed may feel comfortable in some settings and awkward in others. Compare familiar people with unfamiliar audiences.
N4.work: Compare contributing in a small familiar meeting with presenting to an unfamiliar audience.
N4.life: Choose a social setting where you can participate at a comfortable pace.

N5.name: Immoderation
N5.description: Reported difficulty resisting urges or temptations; this is not a diagnosis of addiction or a judgment of character.
N5.low: You report less difficulty resisting temptations. Notice which conditions support your choices rather than assuming willpower is constant.
N5.high: You report more difficulty resisting some urges. For one everyday temptation, try making your preferred choice easier to access.
N5.middle: Resisting an urge may be easier under some conditions than others. Look at tiredness, access and routines around one everyday temptation.
N5.work: Notice which distractions are easiest to act on, and change access to one that interrupts your work.
N5.life: For one everyday temptation, change the surroundings before relying on willpower.

N6.name: Vulnerability
N6.description: Reported tendency to feel overwhelmed or less able to cope under pressure.
N6.low: You report feeling relatively capable under pressure. Still check whether you need information, rest, or help for the particular situation.
N6.high: You report more difficulty under pressure. Breaking one demand into a next step and clarifying available support may be worth trying.
N6.middle: Your sense of coping may depend on the kind of pressure and the support available. Compare two recent demanding situations.
N6.work: For a demanding task, clarify the next step and who can help if you get stuck.
N6.life: When several demands arrive together, separate what needs action now from what can wait.

E1.name: Friendliness
E1.description: Reported warmth and ease in approaching people; it does not measure kindness.
E1.low: You may approach people more reservedly. A brief expression of interest can make your intentions easier for others to read.
E1.high: You may readily express warmth. Check whether a new acquaintance welcomes the same pace of connection.
E1.middle: You may approach people differently depending on familiarity and setting. Notice when warmth comes easily and when you prefer more distance.
E1.work: Notice whether colleagues can read your interest from how you approach them.
E1.life: Express interest in a way that feels natural, while checking the other person’s preferred pace.

E2.name: Gregariousness
E2.description: Reported preference for company, groups, and social gatherings.
E2.low: You may prefer smaller gatherings or more time alone. Suggest the kinds of connection you enjoy rather than only declining others.
E2.high: You may enjoy frequent company and groups. Plan social time while checking that quieter commitments also get attention.
E2.middle: Company and time alone may both appeal to you. Group size, familiarity and the activity may explain which you prefer.
E2.work: Compare individual focus time with collaborative time when planning a working day.
E2.life: Plan a form of connection you actually enjoy, rather than assuming every gathering suits you.

E3.name: Assertiveness
E3.description: Reported willingness to speak up, take charge, and influence group direction.
E3.low: You may be less inclined to take the lead. Prepare one clear request or contribution when your perspective needs to be heard.
E3.high: You may readily influence a discussion. Invite an alternative view before treating your preferred direction as the group's decision.
E3.middle: You may speak up or take the lead selectively. Compare a subject you know well with one where you prefer to listen first.
E3.work: Before a discussion, decide what contribution you want heard and how you will invite other views.
E3.life: Make one preference explicit when agreeing on a shared plan.

E4.name: Activity Level
E4.description: Reported preference for a busy pace and active involvement; this is not a measure of health or productivity.
E4.low: You may prefer a less hurried pace. Allow realistic transition time when planning several commitments.
E4.high: You may enjoy a full, active schedule. Check whether the pace leaves enough room to finish tasks and respond to surprises.
E4.middle: A busy pace may suit some days, while a slower pace suits others. Notice which commitments energise you and which create overload.
E4.work: Plan commitments at a pace that leaves room for transitions and unexpected work.
E4.life: Compare a full day with a quieter day and notice which pace you prefer.

E5.name: Excitement-Seeking
E5.description: Reported appetite for stimulation and exciting experiences; it does not establish reckless behavior.
E5.low: You may prefer less intense stimulation. Choose settings that let you engage comfortably without assuming novelty will be unpleasant.
E5.high: You may enjoy stimulating experiences. Consider the practical consequences separately from how exciting an option feels.
E5.middle: Your appetite for stimulation may vary by experience. Separate interest in novelty from comfort with noise, intensity or risk.
E5.work: Distinguish the stimulation you enjoy from the interruptions that make a task harder.
E5.life: Choose an enjoyable experience and assess its practical consequences separately from its excitement.

E6.name: Cheerfulness
E6.description: Reported tendency to experience and express positive feelings; it is not a complete measure of well-being.
E6.low: You endorsed fewer strongly upbeat statements. A quieter emotional style does not mean you cannot enjoy meaningful experiences.
E6.high: You endorsed more upbeat statements. Your enthusiasm may be welcome; also leave space for someone else's disappointment or concern.
E6.middle: Positive feelings may vary across situations or be expressed quietly. Notice what you enjoy without requiring constant enthusiasm.
E6.work: Notice how your emotional expression affects the tone of a team conversation.
E6.life: Share an enjoyable moment in your own style, leaving room for other people’s feelings.

O1.name: Imagination
O1.description: Reported engagement with fantasy and imagined possibilities.
O1.low: You may prefer concrete information. Sketching one alternative can still be useful when the current approach is stuck.
O1.high: You may readily imagine alternatives. Capture a promising idea in a small practical form to see what it offers.
O1.middle: Concrete thinking and imagined possibilities may both be useful to you. Compare how you approach a practical task and an open-ended idea.
O1.work: For an open problem, compare a concrete example with one alternative you can imagine.
O1.life: Try making one imagined possibility concrete through a sketch, note or small trial.

O2.name: Artistic Interests
O2.description: Reported appreciation of art, beauty, and aesthetic experiences; it does not measure artistic ability.
O2.low: Artistic experiences may be a smaller part of your interests. This says nothing about your ability to learn an art or craft.
O2.high: Aesthetic experiences may matter to you. Consider making intentional room for the forms you actually enjoy.
O2.middle: Your aesthetic interests may be selective. Particular music, places or art forms may matter more than a broad interest in art.
O2.work: Notice whether the appearance of your surroundings affects your experience of working there.
O2.life: Make room for an aesthetic experience you enjoy; no artistic skill is required.

O3.name: Emotionality
O3.description: Reported awareness of and attention to one's feelings; this differs from emotional distress or empathy.
O3.low: You may give feelings less attention when describing experience. Naming a feeling can sometimes clarify what matters in a decision.
O3.high: You may attend closely to your feelings. Treat them as information alongside the facts and practical constraints of a situation.
O3.middle: Attention to feelings may depend on the situation. Compare decisions where you notice your emotions with those where practical facts dominate.
O3.work: When making a decision, identify both the facts and how you feel about the options.
O3.life: Name a feeling and the situation around it without treating it as the whole explanation.

O4.name: Adventurousness
O4.description: Reported willingness to try unfamiliar activities and depart from routine.
O4.low: Familiar activities may appeal more. If a change is needed, a small trial can make the experience easier to evaluate.
O4.high: You may welcome unfamiliar experiences. Check whether a shared change also works for the people affected by it.
O4.middle: You may welcome some changes while preferring familiar routines elsewhere. Notice what makes an unfamiliar activity worth trying.
O4.work: For a change in routine, agree on a small trial and what would make it worth keeping.
O4.life: Compare a familiar activity with one small unfamiliar variation.

O5.name: Intellect
O5.description: A historical label for interest in abstract ideas and intellectual exploration; this is not an IQ or ability score.
O5.low: Abstract discussion may appeal less than concrete problems. This does not imply lower intelligence or less expertise.
O5.high: You may enjoy exploring complex ideas. Translate your reasoning into a concrete example when communicating it to others.
O5.middle: Interest in abstract ideas may depend on the topic and its relevance. This result says nothing about your intelligence.
O5.work: Choose a concrete example when explaining an abstract idea to a colleague.
O5.life: Explore a topic that interests you without treating this score as a measure of intelligence.

O6.name: Liberalism
O6.description: A historical facet combining political and conventional beliefs, including liberal or conservative candidates, crime policy, and absolute right and wrong. These culturally specific items do not establish party membership or voting behavior.
O6.low: You may place more value on established conventions. Consider the reason for a rule when deciding whether it still serves its purpose.
O6.high: You may be inclined to question conventions. Explain what a proposed alternative would improve and how it could be evaluated.
O6.middle: These culturally specific answers are mixed. They cannot establish a political identity; consider the individual beliefs rather than a general label.
O6.work: These culturally specific items do not support advice about job fit. Examine a particular rule on its merits.
O6.life: Consider a specific convention and what it does for the people affected; avoid drawing conclusions about voting.

A1.name: Trust
A1.description: Reported expectation that other people generally have good intentions.
A1.low: You may be cautious about others' intentions. Look for observable evidence before drawing a conclusion about a particular person.
A1.high: You may readily expect good intentions. For important commitments, combine goodwill with clear agreements and follow-through.
A1.middle: Trust may depend on the person and the stakes. Compare initial expectations with the evidence you use before an important commitment.
A1.work: For an important handoff, combine expectations about people with clear ownership and a check-in.
A1.life: Compare a first impression with evidence from the person’s actions.

A2.name: Morality
A2.description: A historical label concerning reported straightforwardness versus strategic self-presentation; it does not measure moral worth.
A2.low: You may be more guarded or strategic in what you disclose. Check that others still have the information needed for a fair agreement.
A2.high: You may favor straightforward communication. Consider timing and privacy as well as candor when sharing sensitive information.
A2.middle: How openly you communicate may depend on trust, privacy and the situation. This score is not a judgment of your moral worth.
A2.work: Clarify what someone needs to know for a fair agreement, while respecting confidentiality.
A2.life: Explain a preference honestly while choosing an appropriate time and level of detail.

A3.name: Altruism
A3.description: Reported willingness to help others and enjoyment of being useful.
A3.low: Helping may be a more selective commitment for you. Make expectations clear so others know what support they can count on.
A3.high: You may readily offer help. Check what the person actually wants and what you can sustainably provide.
A3.middle: You may offer help selectively, depending on capacity and the request. Notice when helping feels worthwhile and when a limit is needed.
A3.work: Before offering help, check both the request and your available capacity.
A3.life: Ask what support is wanted before deciding what to offer.

A4.name: Cooperation
A4.description: Reported willingness to compromise and avoid interpersonal confrontation.
A4.low: You may be willing to confront disagreement. Focus the challenge on the issue and keep a route to resolution open.
A4.high: You may prefer compromise. State an important concern early so agreement reflects your needs as well as others'.
A4.middle: You may compromise on some issues and challenge others. Notice which disagreements deserve a clear position and which allow flexibility.
A4.work: In a disagreement, identify the point you need resolved and what you can compromise on.
A4.life: State one important need before agreeing to a shared decision.

A5.name: Modesty
A5.description: Reported comfort with self-promotion and claims of personal superiority; it is not a measure of confidence or worth.
A5.low: You may be comfortable highlighting your strengths. Use concrete evidence and acknowledge others' contributions when describing success.
A5.high: You may avoid drawing attention to your achievements. A factual account of your contribution can help others understand your work.
A5.middle: Comfort with highlighting your contribution may vary by setting. Compare sharing a factual achievement with making a broad claim about yourself.
A5.work: Describe your contribution using concrete outcomes and acknowledge others’ work.
A5.life: Notice when sharing an achievement helps someone know you better.

A6.name: Sympathy
A6.description: Reported tender concern for others and attention to their difficulties.
A6.low: You may put more weight on detached or practical considerations. Ask about the personal impact before deciding what help is useful.
A6.high: You may be strongly moved by others' difficulties. Clarify what support is wanted and which responsibilities you can reasonably take on.
A6.middle: You may weigh personal feelings and practical considerations differently across situations. Notice how both inform your response to another person.
A6.work: Before solving a problem, ask how it affects the person who brought it to you.
A6.life: Balance concern with a clear account of the support you can provide.

C1.name: Self-Efficacy
C1.description: Reported belief in one's ability to handle tasks effectively; it does not directly measure competence.
C1.low: You may feel less certain of your effectiveness. Review one specific task and identify what knowledge or support would help.
C1.high: You may feel capable of handling tasks. Check that your confidence is supported by the information and preparation this task requires.
C1.middle: Confidence in handling tasks may vary with experience and preparation. Identify one task you feel ready for and one where support would help.
C1.work: For a task you are unsure about, identify the preparation or feedback that would help.
C1.life: Check your confidence against one concrete example of what you have handled before.

C2.name: Orderliness
C2.description: Reported preference for organization, tidiness, and structured surroundings.
C2.low: You may tolerate a less structured environment. Use a simple place or reminder for items whose loss creates real friction.
C2.high: You may prefer clear organization. Distinguish the structure that helps from details that others need not arrange your way.
C2.middle: You may prefer structure in some areas and tolerate disorder in others. Identify which arrangements actually save you time or friction.
C2.work: Choose one arrangement that makes important materials easier to find.
C2.life: Agree on a useful level of order in a shared space without treating preference as a universal standard.

C3.name: Dutifulness
C3.description: Reported commitment to obligations and rules; it does not establish trustworthiness in every situation.
C3.low: You may treat obligations or rules more flexibly. Clarify commitments others rely on before changing them.
C3.high: You may take obligations seriously. Revisit an agreement openly when changed circumstances make the original commitment unrealistic.
C3.middle: Your approach to obligations may depend on the commitment and its purpose. Notice which promises you treat as fixed and which you renegotiate.
C3.work: Make a commitment explicit and renegotiate it early if circumstances change.
C3.life: Choose a reminder for one promise another person relies on.

C4.name: Achievement-Striving
C4.description: Reported drive to meet ambitious standards and pursue accomplishment.
C4.low: Ambitious achievement may be less central to your priorities. Define success around what you actually value and need to accomplish.
C4.high: You may pursue demanding goals. Set a clear stopping point and check what other priorities the effort displaces.
C4.middle: Ambition may be selective rather than constant. Identify the goals that matter to you and those where a sufficient result is enough.
C4.work: Define what success and sufficient completion mean before spending more effort.
C4.life: Check what a demanding goal displaces and whether the trade-off matches your priorities.

C5.name: Self-Discipline
C5.description: Reported ability to begin and persist with tasks despite boredom or distraction.
C5.low: You may find some tasks difficult to start or sustain. Try a small first action with a visible cue and a short work period.
C5.high: You may persist with tasks readily. Pause occasionally to check that completing the task still serves the current priority.
C5.middle: Starting and persisting may depend on interest, clarity or distractions. Compare one task you completed with one you kept postponing.
C5.work: Make the next action small and visible, then check whether your working conditions help you start.
C5.life: For one recurring task, choose a realistic cue and a short starting period.

C6.name: Cautiousness
C6.description: Reported tendency to deliberate before acting; it does not measure decision accuracy.
C6.low: You may decide quickly. For a consequential choice, add one check of the likely downside before committing.
C6.high: You may weigh decisions carefully. Set a decision deadline when further information is unlikely to change the choice.
C6.middle: You may deliberate more for some decisions than others. Notice whether your time spent thinking matches the consequences of the choice.
C6.work: Match time spent deliberating to the consequences and reversibility of the decision.
C6.life: For one choice, decide what information is enough and when you will decide.

pattern.mixed: Within this trait, the highest raw facet mean is {high} ({highScore}/5), while the lowest is {low} ({lowScore}/5). The overall average hides this difference in your responses. Read these tendencies together rather than treating the trait as a single description.
pattern.close: The six facet means are less than one response point apart. No large contrast appears within this trait; the individual descriptions below still show what each part covers.
